planting.note: Sow seed in fall and allow winter cold to break dormancy, or plant nursery-grown mats in spring into a lean, gritty, sharply drained scree or trough mix in full sun; the feathery seed heads are ornamental but germination from collected seed is slow and erratic.

directions: White Mountain Avens forms a slowly spreading woody mat of small, dark-green, scalloped evergreen leaves with felted white undersides, studded in late spring and early summer with upward-facing, eight-petaled white flowers followed by showy twisted silvery seed plumes. It is a dominant, long-lived subshrub of exposed fellfields, rocky ridges, and wind-scoured alpine tundra across the circumpolar north and the high Rockies, thriving where most perennials cannot survive the combination of intense wind, cold, and thin gravelly soil. Plant into a lean, mineral, sharply drained scree, trough, or rock-garden crevice in full sun; established mats are extremely drought- and cold-hardy but resent heavy, wet, or rich soils. Named clones are usually propagated by division or cuttings since seed-grown plants are variable and slow to establish.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall for natural winter stratification, or plant divisions in spring into moist, gritty, well-drained alpine turf soil in full sun; this species forms one of the dominant ground covers of true alpine tundra and establishes faster from seed than most cushion alpines.

directions: Alpine Avens produces tufts of glossy, pinnately divided, fern-like evergreen leaves that often turn bronze-red in fall, topped in early summer by cheerful bright-yellow five-petaled flowers on short stems. It is one of the most abundant and characteristic plants of Rocky Mountain alpine tundra above treeline, frequently forming extensive turf on gentle slopes and snowmelt basins where soil moisture is reliable through early summer. Grow in full sun in gritty, humus-poor but evenly moist, sharply drained soil; it tolerates intense cold, wind, and a short growing season but struggles in hot, humid lowland gardens. Use in rock gardens, troughs, or alpine meadow plantings that mimic its native snowmelt-fed turf habitat.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall and leave exposed to freeze-thaw cycles over winter, since germination is cool-triggered and often spread over more than one season; set out seedlings or divisions into a deep, gritty, humus-rich scree that stays cool and moist in spring.

directions: Alpine Primrose forms tight rosettes of small, gray-green, mealy-backed leaves pressed close to the ground, sending up short stalks in early summer topped by one to several fragrant, rose-pink to magenta flowers with a contrasting yellow eye. It is endemic to the highest rocky tundra, scree, and gravelly turf of the central and southern Rocky Mountains, typically appearing within weeks of snowmelt and depending on that moisture pulse to flower and set seed. Site in full sun in a deep, gritty, well-drained but spring-moist scree or crevice, ideally with a cool root run; it resents summer heat, humidity, and drought and is best suited to true alpine or high-elevation rock gardens. Established plants are long-lived where the climate suits them but are considered a connoisseur's alpine rather than an easy garden plant.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall for winter stratification, or start indoors with 3-4 weeks of moist chilling before moving to a bright, cool spot; transplant into gritty, well-drained rock-garden soil with some afternoon shade at lower elevations.

directions: Dwarf Rocky Mountain Columbine is a diminutive endemic restricted to rocky alpine and upper subalpine crevices in the Front Range and central Colorado mountains, producing dainty, nodding, blue-and-white (occasionally lavender) spurred flowers held just above a low tuft of finely divided, blue-green ferny foliage. Unlike most true cushion alpines it germinates and establishes readily from seed, making it one of the more accessible high-alpine species for rock gardens, troughs, and crevice plantings. Plant in gritty, humus-enriched, sharply drained soil in full sun at high elevation or light afternoon shade in warmer lowland gardens, and keep evenly moist during the growing season. It self-sows modestly where happy but seldom becomes a nuisance, staying a tidy, long-lived rock-garden gem.

planting.note: Nick or lightly scarify the hard seed coat and sow in fall for winter stratification into a lean, gritty, sharply drained scree in full sun; as a legume it benefits from inoculation with a clover-compatible rhizobium if available.

directions: American Alpine Clover forms dense, low cushions of small trifoliate leaflets, topped from early to midsummer by tight, rounded heads of white to pale purple pea flowers often tinged pink at the base. It is a true tundra specialist of exposed fellfields, rocky ridges, and wind-scoured turf above treeline in the central and southern Rocky Mountains, enduring intense cold, wind, and a very short growing season. Grow in a lean, mineral, sharply drained scree or trough in full sun; it is slow-growing and rarely offered in the trade, appearing mainly as wild-collected or seed-exchange material for dedicated alpine and crevice gardens. Avoid rich soil and summer humidity, both of which quickly cause rot in cultivation.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown rooted divisions or cuttings into a deep, gritty scree or crevice mix in full sun; seed germination is slow and erratic, so most garden stock is propagated vegetatively from established cushions.

directions: Cushion Phlox builds an extremely tight, hard mat of small gray-green needle-like leaves, so densely packed it resembles a rounded stone from a distance until smothered in white to pale lavender-pink flowers in early summer. It is native to exposed, rocky alpine fellfields and wind-blasted ridges of the central and southern Rocky Mountains, where its dwarf stature and dense habit shed wind and cold with minimal surface exposure. Plant into a deep, sharply drained scree, trough, or crevice bed in full sun, and avoid any standing moisture at the crown, especially over winter. Extremely slow-growing and long-lived once established, it is a prized but demanding subject for true alpine and crevice gardens.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall and expose to winter freeze-thaw cycles for germination the following spring, planting into a deep scree or gravel bed that lets the massive taproot run down to cool, slightly moist subsoil while the crown stays dry.

directions: Alpine Springbeauty anchors a fleshy rosette of thick, spoon-shaped, water-storing leaves with an enormous carrot-like taproot that can persist for decades, pushing up a tight cluster of white to pink-veined flowers on short stalks soon after snowmelt. It is one of the highest-growing vascular plants in the Rocky Mountains, colonizing the loosest talus, scree, and summit fellfields where almost nothing else can root, often within sight of mountain peaks above 13,000 feet. In cultivation it demands a very deep, sharply drained scree or crevice bed that allows the taproot to reach cool, barely moist subsoil while the crown and foliage stay dry and cold-exposed. It is notoriously difficult outside dedicated alpine-house or deep-bed conditions and is considered an advanced grower's plant rather than a routine garden subject.
